source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

coverage.assignment: Lubbers syllabus VI.C(3), Standing of the Plaintiff to Sue, pp. 721–744
coverage.sourceLimit: Bost v. Illinois State Bd. of Elections (2026 supplement p. 49) and an older-edition p. 753 problem are separately assigned on Canvas but not in uploaded Chapter 11.

topics.title: § 11.1.1 — Background and History of Standing (pp. 721–723)
topics.description: Traditional legal-wrong test versus statutory authorization for competitive and other indirect injuries.

entries.title: Standing is easy for regulated target, harder for indirect victim
entries.summary: The person directly bound by a rule, order, license denial, or sanction ordinarily can challenge it; a third-party beneficiary or competitor usually must prove concrete injury, causation and redressability.
entries.laymanExplanation: A business fined by agency can usually sue. A nearby competitor harmed by the agency's decision about someone else has additional hurdles.
entries.legalExplanation: Regulation of third parties introduces intervening choices. Distinguish object of agency action from beneficiary/competitor who challenges it.
entries.examApplication: Classify target/indirect challenger at outset.
entries.examTrap: A third party can have standing, but cannot assume a regulatory violation alone gives it standing.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Historical legal-wrong test
entries.summary: Traditionally courts required invasion of legal right recognized at common law or statute; mere injury from new competition did not count.
entries.laymanExplanation: Losing customers because of a government-approved competitor wasn't itself a legal wrong.
entries.legalExplanation: Tennessee Electric Power rejected competitors' challenge to TVA operations absent protected right against competition. Modern APA and Article III doctrines are different.
entries.examApplication: Use as history and contrast ADAPSO, Sanders and APA § 702.
entries.examTrap: Do not apply pre-1970 legal-right test as today's universal federal APA rule.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Tennessee Electric Power Co. v. TVA, 306 U.S. 118 (1939)
entries.summary: Power companies lacked legal-wrong standing to stop TVA competition, despite constitutional objection to governmental power generation.
entries.laymanExplanation: Government-backed competitor hurts profits but that alone did not confer historic legal right.
entries.legalExplanation: This is textbook background, not governing modern ADAPSO approach.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook Notes and Questions; full judicial opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Statutory competitor standing and private attorney general
entries.summary: Congress may authorize review by persons 'aggrieved' by agency licensing even absent common-law right against competition, allowing vindication of public law.
entries.laymanExplanation: A statute can let a competitor challenge agency's unlawful license even though competition is ordinarily lawful.
entries.legalExplanation: Sanders Brothers radio station could challenge competing FCC license under Communications Act; Hardin involved statute meant to protect competitors.
entries.examApplication: Find statutory review clause, protected interests and separate Article III minimum.
entries.examTrap: Congress's authorization to sue cannot erase Article III's concrete-injury requirement.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: FCC v. Sanders Brothers Radio Station, 309 U.S. 470 (1940)
entries.summary: FCC license competitor suffered economic injury and statute authorized 'aggrieved' review notwithstanding no common-law protection from competition.
entries.laymanExplanation: Statutory access widens legal-wrong standing.
entries.legalExplanation: Example of private attorney general enforcing proper statutory administration.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook Notes and Questions; full judicial opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Hardin v. Kentucky Utilities Co., 390 U.S. 1 (1968)
entries.summary: Competitor standing supported where Congress enacted protection for class of competitors.
entries.laymanExplanation: Legislative intention to safeguard competitors matters.
entries.legalExplanation: Separate injury to business from statutory right to seek review.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook Notes and Questions; full judicial opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Standing as contested gatekeeping
entries.summary: Textbook asks whether threshold standing rulings sometimes substitute for judicial decisions on difficult merits, and highlights judicial-administrative resource tradeoffs.
entries.laymanExplanation: Judges may disagree over who gets in the courthouse before discussing whether agency was right.
entries.legalExplanation: Useful policy framing but not a stand-alone doctrinal test.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

topics.title: § 11.1.2 — Article III Standing; Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife (pp. 723–728)
topics.description: Constitutional injury, causation, redressability, third-party choices, procedural rights, separate opinions.

entries.title: Three-part Article III standing test
entries.summary: Plaintiff must prove (1) concrete, particularized, actual or imminent injury in fact; (2) harm fairly traceable to challenged agency conduct; and (3) likelihood that favorable judicial decision will redress harm.
entries.laymanExplanation: Show a real personal injury, caused by what government did, that a judge can realistically fix.
entries.legalExplanation: Article III case-or-controversy requirement is jurisdictional; courts decide it before merits. Burden of producing specific proof increases at summary judgment and trial.
entries.examApplication: Write three distinct elements and tie each to facts; classify present versus future injury and causal third parties.
entries.examTrap: An agency violation by itself does not satisfy all three elements.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Standing is threshold even when merits easier
entries.summary: Federal courts must address Article III standing before reaching merits, even if agency claim seems plainly meritless.
entries.laymanExplanation: Court cannot say plaintiff loses on law if the plaintiff lacks power to be in federal court.
entries.legalExplanation: Steel Co. requires independent subject-matter jurisdiction analysis rather than hypothetical jurisdiction.
entries.examApplication: Answer Article III before zone of interests and lawfulness.
entries.examTrap: Standing is different from winning case on merits.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
entries.summary: No. Members failed to show imminent personal injury; generalized interest in endangered species and abstract procedural entitlement were insufficient. Scalia's separate redressability analysis in Part III.B was joined by only three Justices and is not a majority holding.
entries.laymanExplanation: Article III requires personal, concrete and imminent injury, fairly traceable and likely redressable; abstract general procedural grievance alone is inadequate even when statute permits 'any person' to sue.
entries.legalExplanation: Prior travel and unspecified 'some day' return did not show actual/imminent personal injury. Ecological, animal and professional interest nexus theories swept too broadly. Citizen-suit legislation cannot convert every person's general interest in governmental compliance into a concrete injury. Third-party foreign project funding raised further redressability difficulty, though the relevant opinion part was only a plurality.
entries.examApplication: Describe members' specific travel plans, physical use of area, administrative consultation, foreign actors and precise relief. Explain Kennedy concurrence versus dissent as relevant.
entries.examTrap: Never label Scalia's Part III.B redressability discussion a majority holding; do not assume aesthetic harm is categorically noncognizable.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpt in assigned chapter
entries.facts: Environmental organization challenged Interior Department regulation exempting overseas U.S.-funded projects from ESA consultation. Members had previously traveled to Sri Lanka and Egypt and hoped to return someday to see endangered elephants, leopards and crocodiles, but identified no concrete return dates. Funding agencies and foreign project operators were not defendants.
entries.issue: Did aesthetic interest and indefinite intentions to revisit affected animal habitat, combined with ESA citizen-suit right, establish Article III standing to challenge omission of overseas consultation?
entries.holding: No. Members failed to show imminent personal injury; generalized interest in endangered species and abstract procedural entitlement were insufficient. Scalia's separate redressability analysis in Part III.B was joined by only three Justices and is not a majority holding.
entries.reasoning: Prior travel and unspecified 'some day' return did not show actual/imminent personal injury. Ecological, animal and professional interest nexus theories swept too broadly. Citizen-suit legislation cannot convert every person's general interest in governmental compliance into a concrete injury. Third-party foreign project funding raised further redressability difficulty, though the relevant opinion part was only a plurality.
entries.rule: Article III requires personal, concrete and imminent injury, fairly traceable and likely redressable; abstract general procedural grievance alone is inadequate even when statute permits 'any person' to sue.

entries.title: Indirectly harmed challengers bear a heavier factual burden
entries.summary: When agency regulates or fails to regulate somebody else, causation and redressability depend on nonparty actors' independent behavior.
entries.laymanExplanation: Court cannot automatically assume a private company will respond as plaintiff hopes if agency changes policy.
entries.legalExplanation: Lujan distinguished direct object of agency regulation from downstream third-party beneficiaries and required evidence of actual/predictable choices.
entries.examApplication: Lay out causal chain and specify each independent choice.
entries.examTrap: Nonparty involvement increases difficulty but does not create categorical ban on standing.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Aesthetic and environmental injury is cognizable when personal
entries.summary: Use or enjoyment of wildlife can count as injury, but plaintiff must show herself actually or imminently affected in particular location.
entries.laymanExplanation: You may sue over harm to your own planned hike or wildlife viewing, not merely because you care about animals.
entries.legalExplanation: Lujan rejected unspecific 'some day' trip allegations and overly general 'ecosystem nexus', 'animal nexus', and 'vocational nexus'.
entries.examApplication: Ask where plaintiff personally goes, how harm affects actual use, and when next visit is concrete.
entries.examTrap: A conservation organization's history of advocacy does not substitute for an injured member.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Procedural injury must protect separate concrete interest
entries.summary: A plaintiff may enforce procedural rights affecting her real interests with relaxed aspects of immediacy and redressability, but not demand universal compliance for its own sake.
entries.laymanExplanation: You may ask for required environmental review of dam next door, but can't sue just because an agency skipped some procedure anywhere in the world.
entries.legalExplanation: ESA universal citizen-suit clause alone did not create injury for everyone; footnote 7 discusses specific neighbor's dam/environmental impact statement example.
entries.examApplication: Identify harmed environmental, property or economic interest separate from omitted procedure.
entries.examTrap: Congress cannot simply dispense with Article III injury by saying 'any person may sue'.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Lujan separation-of-powers explanation
entries.summary: Majority reasoned that limitless citizen suits would shift the President's Take Care enforcement function toward ongoing judicial supervision of executive branch.
entries.laymanExplanation: Courts should decide concrete disputes, not become general supervisors of every federal agency.
entries.legalExplanation: This is majority rationale for maintaining injury-in-fact requirement, relevant to reviewing agency nonenforcement.
entries.examApplication: Compare private attorney general theory and constitutional limits.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Kennedy-Souter concurrence and dissents
entries.summary: Kennedy/Souter agreed that ESA language was too broad to create concrete personal injury but emphasized Congress can define injuries and causal relationships. Stevens concurred in judgment on foreign ESA reach; Blackmun/O'Connor dissented on evidence and procedural rights.
entries.laymanExplanation: The Justices agreed on dismissal for different reasons; some wanted more room for statutory citizen suits.
entries.legalExplanation: Kennedy's concurrence is important to the votes; Scalia's standalone redressability analysis lacked majority support.
entries.examApplication: Keep constitutional holding versus separate opinions distinct.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

topics.title: § 11.1.2 Notes — Injury, Imminence and Concreteness (pp. 728–731)
topics.description: Public-interest organizations, Sierra Club, Clapper, Monsanto, Spokeo, tangible versus intangible harms.

entries.title: Sierra Club v. Morton, 405 U.S. 727 (1972)
entries.summary: Sierra Club's longstanding commitment to wilderness was insufficient; after pleading actual members' visits to Mineral King, amended complaint cleared initial threshold.
entries.laymanExplanation: Institutional concern about environment isn't enough without somebody personally harmed.
entries.legalExplanation: Book describes Douglas's dissent proposing standing for nature itself; rejected by majority.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook Notes and Questions; full judicial opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Imminence of threatened future injury
entries.summary: Future harm must be certainly impending or carry substantial risk; speculative chains and vague 'some day' intentions fail.
entries.laymanExplanation: Something realistic must be about to harm you—'I might someday suffer' is weak.
entries.legalExplanation: Clapper found conjectural surveillance chain; Monsanto allowed farmers' demonstrated substantial risk of genetically modified alfalfa cross-pollination.
entries.examApplication: Analyze likelihood, steps involving independent actors, concrete future plan and actual risk.
entries.examTrap: Don't treat Clapper 'certainly impending' as abolishing substantial-risk path.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Clapper v. Amnesty International USA, 568 U.S. 398 (2013)
entries.summary: Lawyers and advocates could not show foreign-intelligence surveillance would target their communications; speculative precautions against hypothetical surveillance could not manufacture injury.
entries.laymanExplanation: Spending money to avoid unlikely feared surveillance doesn't automatically prove injury.
entries.legalExplanation: Secret court approval and selection of plaintiffs' communications rested on speculation.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook Notes and Questions; full judicial opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Monsanto Co. v. Geertson Seed Farms, 561 U.S. 139 (2010)
entries.summary: Organic farmers showed substantial risk their crops would be cross-pollinated by modified alfalfa, imposing testing/economic consequences.
entries.laymanExplanation: Realistic biological spillover could justify protective expenses.
entries.legalExplanation: Contrasts Clapper's speculative government surveillance chain.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook Notes and Questions; full judicial opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Concrete injury can be intangible
entries.summary: Injury in fact must be real and nonabstract, but need not be tangible or monetary; informational errors require meaningful injury or recognized close analog.
entries.laymanExplanation: Wrong facts about your background can matter if they plausibly harm you; a harmless typo usually doesn't.
entries.legalExplanation: Spokeo instructed lower court to examine whether erroneous online credit data caused or posed material risk of real harm; bare statutory violation may not suffice.
entries.examApplication: Ask whether actual intangible injury or harm risk is concrete and particularized.
entries.examTrap: Do not equate statutory damages entitlement with automatic Article III injury.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330 (2016)
entries.summary: Online profile misstated plaintiff's age, marital status, work and qualifications. Court remanded for concreteness assessment under FCRA rather than automatically treating statutory noncompliance as injury.
entries.laymanExplanation: Wrong ZIP code may be harmless, but plausible job opportunity damage could be concrete.
entries.legalExplanation: Dissent argued alleged overqualification/foreclosed employment was sufficiently concrete.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook Notes and Questions; full judicial opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Federal public interest standing versus state public actions
entries.summary: Federal Article III ordinarily rejects ideological interest alone; some state courts allow citizen enforcement of public duties by mandamus, while others follow federal-style requirements.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some state courts let ordinary citizens enforce public rights even without unique harm, unlike federal courts.
entries.legalExplanation: California Common Cause accepted voter registration public duty; Ohio and Florida cases rejected broader public action theory.
entries.examApplication: Specify state or federal forum and constitutional standing source.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume all state standing rules copy Article III.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

topics.title: § 11.1.2 Notes — Associations and Membership Standing (pp. 731–732)
topics.description: Hunt requirements, Summers member-specific evidence, FDA v Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine organizational spending.

entries.title: Hunt three-factor associational standing
entries.summary: An association may sue for members when (1) at least one member has individual standing, (2) asserted interest is germane to organization's purpose, (3) claim and relief do not require individual members to participate.
entries.laymanExplanation: The group needs an identifiable injured member and mission-related claim; lawsuit must be workable on group basis.
entries.legalExplanation: Hunt v Washington State Apple Advertising Commission is controlling framework cited by chapter; nonmoney declaratory remedies typically easier for element three.
entries.examApplication: Name at least one member and run Lujan test for that member before other Hunt factors.
entries.examTrap: Do not satisfy member injury by merely stating organization has many members.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Hunt v. Washington State Apple Advertising Commission, 432 U.S. 333 (1977)
entries.summary: Three-part germaneness/member standing/individual participation test.
entries.laymanExplanation: Groups can litigate for members when conditions met.
entries.legalExplanation: Court framework described in notes, not full Hunt opinion.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook Notes and Questions; full judicial opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Summers v. Earth Island Institute, 555 U.S. 488 (2009)
entries.summary: Large Sierra Club membership and statistical probability someone would visit affected forest were insufficient without specific member evidence.
entries.laymanExplanation: Big membership alone doesn't prove a member is injured.
entries.legalExplanation: Member's personal connection and future visits must be shown.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook Notes and Questions; full judicial opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Organization cannot manufacture its own injury by advocacy spending
entries.summary: A nonprofit cannot create direct organizational standing merely by spending resources on research and advocacy against disliked regulation.
entries.laymanExplanation: Choosing to spend money fighting a policy does not make the policy an injury to the organization.
entries.legalExplanation: FDA v Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine rejected costs voluntarily incurred to oppose mifepristone rule as injury attributable to FDA.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish direct operational injury caused by law from discretionary lobbying expenses.
entries.examTrap: Do not mistake the association's litigation costs for injury in fact.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, 602 U.S. 367 (2024)
entries.summary: Medical advocacy group lacked standing based on self-initiated studies and advocacy costs to oppose FDA abortion medication policy.
entries.laymanExplanation: Self-imposed advocacy expenditure insufficient.
entries.legalExplanation: This is note case, no full opinion reproduced.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook Notes and Questions; full judicial opinion not excerpted

topics.title: § 11.1.2 Notes — Traceability, Redressability and Special Plaintiffs (pp. 732–737)
topics.description: Third-party dependence, Massachusetts v EPA, Murthy, United States v Texas, procedural/ informational injury, taxpayer claims.

entries.title: Traceability requires de facto causal connection
entries.summary: Plaintiff must show challenged governmental conduct fairly traces to harm; action by third parties complicates but can be predictable in some contexts.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency policy must actually have a meaningful causal link to harm, even through other actors.
entries.legalExplanation: Department of Commerce census decision credited predictable drop in immigrant responses despite their independent choices.
entries.examApplication: Identify every step between policy and harm; assess whether predictable evidence rather than speculation supports link.
entries.examTrap: But-for speculation that private actors might change behavior isn't enough.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Redressability: favorable judgment must likely help
entries.summary: A court order must likely remedy or materially lessen plaintiff's injury, not just improve undefined odds.
entries.laymanExplanation: Winning should make a realistic difference, not just express disapproval of agency.
entries.legalExplanation: Murthy noted content platforms independently remove speech; wrestling case said schools might not reinstate programs after Title IX policy invalidation.
entries.examApplication: Specify exact order and likely behavior of government and nonparties.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume invalidating agency policy forces independent private actors to reverse all conduct.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Department of Commerce v. New York, 588 U.S. 752 (2019)
entries.summary: States had census-question standing based on predictable noncitizen response reducing enumeration, federal money and congressional representation.
entries.laymanExplanation: Courts sometimes accept evidence-based predictions of third-party responses.
entries.legalExplanation: Contrasts more skeptical handling of independent choices elsewhere.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook Notes and Questions; full judicial opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Murthy v. Missouri, 603 U.S. 43 (2024)
entries.summary: Social media users failed to tie specific platform moderation to federal pressure and show an injunction would redress moderation platforms independently undertook.
entries.laymanExplanation: Showing government talked to platform isn't enough to prove it caused your exact censorship.
entries.legalExplanation: Third-party moderators not defendant; independent moderation history undermined traceability/redressability.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook Notes and Questions; full judicial opinion not excerpted

entries.title: National Wrestling Coaches Ass'n v. Department of Education, 366 F.3d 930 (D.C. Cir. 2004)
entries.summary: Wrestling coaches lacked redressability because colleges might not restore programs after DOE Title IX policy rescission.
entries.laymanExplanation: A favorable ruling might offer only vague 'better odds.'
entries.legalExplanation: Colleges had budget and other motives to drop sports.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook Notes and Questions; full judicial opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Massachusetts v. EPA, 549 U.S. 497 (2007) — standing aspect
entries.summary: Massachusetts showed injury to state coastal land from sea-level rise and received special solicitude as state in climate pollution suit.
entries.laymanExplanation: A state's own coastal property loss counted as personal injury even if one EPA rule helped incrementally.
entries.legalExplanation: Chapter comments on uncertainty of future precedential reach, but does not establish Massachusetts has been overturned.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish incremental reduction of harm from total climate cure.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook Notes and Questions; full judicial opinion not excerpted

entries.title: States as plaintiffs are not always given special solicitude
entries.summary: Massachusetts v EPA accepted state quasi-sovereign standing to address coastal property; United States v Texas rejected standing to demand federal government arrest more immigrants.
entries.laymanExplanation: State cannot automatically sue to force prosecution of someone else.
entries.legalExplanation: Court in US v Texas used limits tied to third-party nonenforcement and did not rely on Massachusetts's quasi-sovereign reasoning.
entries.examApplication: Classify asserted state interest as own property injury versus demand to arrest particular third parties.
entries.examTrap: Don't say state status alone satisfies Article III.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: United States v. Texas, 599 U.S. 670 (2023)
entries.summary: States lacked standing to challenge federal removal prioritization because parties generally cannot compel arrest or prosecution of others.
entries.laymanExplanation: Economic burden on state did not automatically create cognizable right to force enforcement.
entries.legalExplanation: Related to Heckler v Chaney rule.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook Notes and Questions; full judicial opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Procedural right plus concrete interest may relax immediacy/redressability
entries.summary: Environmental neighbor affected by dam can sue for failure to prepare EIS even if eventual approval may remain; must show affected concrete interest.
entries.laymanExplanation: Required study might influence decision, and plaintiff lives beside harm.
entries.legalExplanation: Lujan footnote 7 recognizes procedural claim tied to particular injury; no stand-alone universal procedural compliance right.
entries.examApplication: Identify procedural mandate, protected real interest, and possibility procedure might affect outcome.
entries.examTrap: Don't treat procedural injury as eliminating injury-in-fact.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Statutory informational injury
entries.summary: Congress can create concrete entitlement to information, so denial of statutorily owed disclosure can support standing even when many others similarly deprived.
entries.laymanExplanation: Being denied information law says you should receive can be concrete harm.
entries.legalExplanation: FEC v Akins voter-disclosure injury and FOIA/FACA access examples; contrasted mere procedural right to comment under Summers absent separate harm.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish entitlement to information from abstract demand agency follow rule.
entries.examTrap: Generalized does not necessarily mean nonconcrete when each person is denied specific statutory information.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: FEC v. Akins, 524 U.S. 11 (1998)
entries.summary: Voter denied disclosure campaign-finance statute required could sue despite many voters experiencing same lack of information.
entries.laymanExplanation: A shared injury can still be legally concrete.
entries.legalExplanation: Informational right distinct from generalized policy disagreement.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook Notes and Questions; full judicial opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Taxpayer standing federal versus state
entries.summary: Federal taxpayer generally may not challenge federal spending based solely on taxpayer status; narrow Flast Establishment Clause exception; state/local taxpayer actions vary widely.
entries.laymanExplanation: You can't sue over every federal expense just because you pay taxes; some states grant broader municipal taxpayer suits.
entries.legalExplanation: Flast limited to certain legislative Establishment Clause expenditure challenges; Hein and Winn narrowed. DC courts can use D.C. local taxpayer standards independent of Article III.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish federal taxpayer/municipal taxpayer and claim nature.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume Flast applies to all executive faith-based programs or tax credits.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

topics.title: § 11.1.3 — APA § 702 Zone of Interests; ADAPSO (pp. 737–744)
topics.description: Statutory standing as distinct from Article III, ADAPSO full brief, Clarke, Patchak, Air Courier, third party rights.

entries.title: APA § 702: adversely affected within meaning of relevant statute
entries.summary: Plaintiff must meet Article III injury-in-fact AND show interest arguably within zone protected or regulated by statutory provision at issue; the zone test is statutory, not Article III itself.
entries.laymanExplanation: You can have real financial loss yet be wrong kind of claimant for this statute.
entries.legalExplanation: ADAPSO moved beyond old legal-wrong test; Clarke interprets zone leniently, excluding interests marginally related to or inconsistent with program aims.
entries.examApplication: Apply zone after Article III; read actual regulatory purposes and plaintiff interest.
entries.examTrap: Don't collapse zone test into merits requirement to prove agency actually violated statute.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Association of Data Processing Service Organizations v. Camp (ADAPSO), 397 U.S. 150 (1970)
entries.summary: Yes. They alleged injury in fact and their interests were arguably within zone protected or regulated by banking statutes. Supreme Court remanded for merits decision.
entries.laymanExplanation: APA competitor challengers must have concrete injury and show arguable alignment with statute's regulatory purposes, not common-law legal right against competition.
entries.legalExplanation: Justice Douglas treated the APA as liberalizing legal-wrong test: economic injury can be enough under Article III, while separate statutory inquiry asks if claimant's interests arguably fit relevant statute. Competitors' interests reasonably related to acts limiting bank service businesses. Brennan concurred only in result, criticizing zone test as duplicative of reviewability inquiry.
entries.examApplication: Analyze economic harm, relevance of Bank Service Corporation Act, absence of preclusion, and distinction among standing/reviewability/merits.
entries.examTrap: ADAPSO does not establish that any business hurt by any agency policy meets zone of interests.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpt in assigned chapter
entries.facts: Data-processing companies challenged Comptroller of Currency ruling permitting national banks to sell data-processing services; companies feared losing customers and profits. Lower courts dismissed for lack of standing.
entries.issue: Can a competitor economically injured by banking agency ruling seek APA judicial review without independent common-law right to protection against competition?
entries.holding: Yes. They alleged injury in fact and their interests were arguably within zone protected or regulated by banking statutes. Supreme Court remanded for merits decision.
entries.reasoning: Justice Douglas treated the APA as liberalizing legal-wrong test: economic injury can be enough under Article III, while separate statutory inquiry asks if claimant's interests arguably fit relevant statute. Competitors' interests reasonably related to acts limiting bank service businesses. Brennan concurred only in result, criticizing zone test as duplicative of reviewability inquiry.
entries.rule: APA competitor challengers must have concrete injury and show arguable alignment with statute's regulatory purposes, not common-law legal right against competition.

entries.title: Zone test is lenient but not empty
entries.summary: Courts generally exclude plaintiffs whose interests are marginally related or inconsistent with statute's aims; they do not require proof Congress specifically named claimant as beneficiary.
entries.laymanExplanation: A competitor who fits the law's regulatory concern may sue; a paper supplier harmed by online fund reports likely cannot.
entries.legalExplanation: Clarke and Patchak apply generous 'arguably' test; Twin Rivers Paper excluded plaintiff injured by drop in printing because SEC fund disclosure law concerns investors.
entries.examApplication: Specify statutory objective rather than only complaining plaintiff lost money.
entries.examTrap: Unrelated economic ripple effects do not prove zone of interests.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Clarke v. Securities Industry Association, 479 U.S. 388 (1987)
entries.summary: Zone inquiry not especially demanding; disallow when interests only marginally related or inconsistent with statutory purpose.
entries.laymanExplanation: Benefit of doubt tends to plaintiff if plausible connection.
entries.legalExplanation: Banking/securities competitors case.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook Notes and Questions; full judicial opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Match-E-Be-Nash-She-Wish Band v. Patchak, 567 U.S. 209 (2012)
entries.summary: Neighbor contesting land acquisition for tribal casino met zone test because land-use consequences to neighbors within concerns of Indian Reorganization Act land acquisition.
entries.laymanExplanation: Neighbor economic and aesthetic land-use interest plausibly relevant.
entries.legalExplanation: Court emphasized use of land, not solely title transfer.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook Notes and Questions; full judicial opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Twin Rivers Paper Co. v. SEC, 934 F.3d 607 (D.C. Cir. 2019)
entries.summary: Paper seller financially harmed when SEC authorized online fund reporting but outside investor-protective statute's interests.
entries.laymanExplanation: Economic consequence isn't enough if law protects others.
entries.legalExplanation: Contrast banking competitor.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook Notes and Questions; full judicial opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Air Courier: test sometimes applied restrictively
entries.summary: Postal employees' potential job losses were not interests protected by nineteenth-century Private Express Statutes, which aimed to protect postal monopoly, not jobs.
entries.laymanExplanation: Workers could really lose work yet be outside the statute's protected scope.
entries.legalExplanation: Court refused to use unrelated 1970 postal labor statute as relevant statute; casebook contrasts Patchak/Clarke's lenience.
entries.examApplication: Identify exact statutory provision versus broader regulatory field.
entries.examTrap: Don't make zone satisfied by citing any statute concerning same agency.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Air Courier Conference of America v. American Postal Workers Union, 498 U.S. 517 (1991)
entries.summary: Postal workers failed zone test for challenge to USPS permission for private international couriers despite job-loss injury.
entries.laymanExplanation: Purpose of 1792/1845 law wasn't employment protection.
entries.legalExplanation: Tension with more generous zone cases.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook Notes and Questions; full judicial opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Lexmark: zone of interests treated as statutory cause-of-action question
entries.summary: Supreme Court extended zone reasoning beyond APA to statutorily created causes of action, grounded in who Congress authorized to sue.
entries.laymanExplanation: Whether you're among people a statute lets sue is different from whether Constitution lets a court hear your injury.
entries.legalExplanation: Lexmark v Static Control reaffirmed lenient zone approach; text's date citation inconsistent across references, but substantive premise is stable.
entries.examApplication: Use statute-specific statutory review or cause-of-action test after standing.
entries.examTrap: Avoid calling every statutory zone question an Article III jurisdiction prerequisite.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Zone test in state administrative law
entries.summary: States split: Illinois and Iowa reject zone test in favor of injury; New York, Florida and Pennsylvania may apply zone principles even if statutes omit federal § 702 text.
entries.laymanExplanation: State approaches can demand different proof beyond actual injury.
entries.legalExplanation: Society of Plastics rejected bag makers' EIS challenge because environmental process law protects local environmental interest; Sun-Brite rejected business competition under zoning law.
entries.examApplication: Check controlling state statutory language and precedent.
entries.examTrap: No uniform state zone test.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Jus tertii: third-party standing restriction
entries.summary: Ordinarily plaintiff must assert own rights; exceptions can arise for close relationships or practical/legal barriers preventing the true rights-holder from suing.
entries.laymanExplanation: You usually can't sue only about someone else's rights, unless strong legal relationship or barrier justifies it.
entries.legalExplanation: Book mentions doctor-patient and vendor-purchaser as examples; keep distinct from organizational Hunt standing.
entries.examApplication: Identify rights-holder and exception, not simply whose interests plaintiff cares about.
entries.examTrap: Third-party standing is separate from standing based on plaintiff's own injury.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Brennan's ADAPSO concurrence: zone is really reviewability
entries.summary: Brennan would analyze Article III injury, then ask separately whether Congress barred claims by this plaintiff, without a duplicative standing hurdle.
entries.laymanExplanation: He wanted one constitutional standing question and statutory reviewability question, not two labels over same law.
entries.legalExplanation: This is concurrence, not controlling ADAPSO majority.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 721–744 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
